title: Opinions with reasons
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: creo que takes the INDICATIVE and no creo que takes the SUBJUNCTIVE: creo que es fácil, no creo que sea fácil. English keeps one shape for both — "I think it is" and "I don't think it is" — so the negative is where an English speaker writes the wrong verb, every time, without anything in the sentence warning them.

Four cells and no more: sea (ser), tenga (tener), pueda (poder), vaya (ir). Each is built off the yo form of the indicative — tengo → tenga, puedo → pueda — except sea and vaya, which are learnt whole. One cell covers yo and él/ella both, so no creo que sea fácil takes its subject from the conversation. The mood as a system, and every other trigger, is a later level's.

Spanish softens an opinion with the FRAME, not with the claim: me parece que, la verdad es que, no sé si. None of them weakens what follows; they place it. An English speaker who softens the claim itself — "it might be a little bit wrong" — sounds evasive in Spanish rather than polite, because the hedging lands on the fact instead of on the speaker.

An equal comparison is written tan + adjective + como, one piece with a gap in the middle: tan difícil como el otro. The como that closes it is part of the frame; it is not L1-M4's como, "I eat", and it is not the que that más and menos take.

aunque joins a concession to a claim and here it takes the INDICATIVE, because what it concedes is a fact: estoy de acuerdo, aunque es caro. It works at either end of the sentence. The subjunctive after aunque — the "even if" reading, about something not yet true — is a later level's.

sentences.display: Creo que es fácil. No creo que sea fácil.
sentences.cue: I think it's easy. I don't think it's easy.
sentences.literal: I-believe that is easy. Not I-believe that be easy.

words.note: The subjunctive of ser — the shape no creo que forces. One cell covers yo and él/ella both, so no creo que sea fácil takes its subject from the conversation.
One ending for both genders, like grande: un examen fácil, una hermana fácil de entender. The plural adds -es and the accent stays where it was: fáciles.

sentences.trap: The English is the same sentence twice with a not in it. The Spanish is not: negating the believing reaches all the way into the second verb and changes its shape.
sentences.sound: FA-sil, stressed on the first syllable, which is exactly what the accent mark is there to say. SE-a is two syllables and both vowels are said.

variations.cue: I think it's hard.
variations.changed: the adjective, with the indicative untouched

variations.cue: I don't think it's hard.
variations.changed: the same swap on the negative side, where sea stays

mistake.why: no creo que forces the subjunctive: no creo que sea fácil. es is the shape creo que would have taken, and it is the first thing an English speaker writes.

sentences.usage: The module's whole grammar in one item, and the pair to say out loud until the second half stops feeling like an extra step.
sentences.mnemonic: Doubt it and the verb changes.

sentences.display: Mi jefe cree que tiene tiempo. No creo que tenga tiempo.
sentences.cue: My boss thinks he has time. I don't think he has time.
sentences.literal: My boss believes that has time. Not I-believe that have time.

words.note: The subjunctive of tener, built off the yo form tengo rather than off the infinitive — which is where the g comes from: tengo, tenga.
Time as an amount of it: tengo tiempo, no tengo tiempo. The hour on a clock is L1-M4's hora, and the two never swap places.

sentences.trap: cree que and no creo que sit in one item on purpose. Somebody else's belief is still a belief, so it keeps the indicative; only the negation flips the mood.
sentences.sound: TEN-ga, with a hard g as in "go" — the e in front of it never softens it. TIEM-po in two syllables, the ie said as one glide.

variations.cue: I don't think he's hungry.
variations.changed: what is not had

variations.cue: I think he has a problem.
variations.changed: back to the indicative, with a new object

mistake.why: The negated belief reaches the second verb: no creo que tenga tiempo. tiene is correct only under creo que, four words earlier in this same item.

sentences.usage: Disagreeing with somebody who is not in the room, which is most of what an opinion frame is for at work.

sentences.display: Me parece que puede ayudar. No creo que pueda hoy.
sentences.cue: It seems to me he can help. I don't think he can today.
sentences.literal: To-me seems that can to-help. Not I-believe that can today.

words.cue: it seems to me · I think
words.note: The softest of the opinion frames, and a positive one: it takes the indicative exactly as creo que does. It places the claim as yours rather than weakening it.
The subjunctive of poder, built off the yo form puedo: puedo, pueda. L2-M1's puede is the indicative and nothing about it changes here.

sentences.trap: Softening in Spanish is a frame in front of the claim. me parece que does not make the helping less likely; it makes the sentence an opinion instead of a report.
sentences.sound: me pa-RE-se, four quick syllables and no pause after me. PUE-da, the ue said as one glide.

variations.cue: I think it's interesting.
variations.changed: the frame over an opinion instead of an ability

variations.cue: I don't think he can help.
variations.changed: the subjunctive half given its verb back

mistake.why: me parece que is a positive frame and takes the indicative: me parece que es interesante. Only a negated belief flips the mood, and this module is where that over-correction is learnt.

sentences.usage: The frame to reach for when you are giving an opinion to somebody who did not ask for one.
sentences.mnemonic: me parece places it; it does not weaken it.

sentences.display: Creo que vamos al cine. No creo que vaya hoy.
sentences.cue: I think we're going to the cinema. I don't think I'll go today.
sentences.literal: I-believe that we-go to-the cinema. Not I-believe that go today.

words.note: The subjunctive of ir. It looks nothing like voy, vas or vamos, so it is learnt whole rather than built — and one cell covers yo and él/ella.

sentences.trap: vaya is the one cell of the four with no visible parent. voy gives nothing away, which is why the module puts it beside vamos in the same breath.
sentences.sound: BA-ya, with the v said as a soft b and the ll-sound of the y — the same sound as in yo.

variations.display: No creo que vaya al cine.
variations.cue: I don't think I'll go to the cinema.
variations.changed: the destination restored

variations.cue: I think we're going on Saturday.
variations.changed: the day instead of the place

mistake.display: No creo que voy al cine.
mistake.why: voy is the indicative and the frame forces vaya: no creo que vaya al cine. Nothing in voy hints at the shape, which is why this one has to be memorised.

sentences.usage: Backing out of a plan without saying no. The negative belief is the softening, and Spanish hears it as one.
sentences.mnemonic: voy tells you nothing; vaya is learnt whole.

sentences.display: Este libro no es tan difícil como el otro.
sentences.cue: This book isn't as hard as the other one.
sentences.literal: This book not is so hard as the other.

words.note: as … as, written around the adjective: tan difícil como el otro. The como that closes it belongs to this frame, not to L1-M4's como, "I eat".
One ending for both genders, and the accent stays put in the plural: difíciles. Built exactly like fácil, and its opposite.

sentences.trap: L2-M9 bought más difícil que and menos difícil que. An EQUAL comparison drops que entirely and closes with como instead, and the two frames never mix.
sentences.sound: tan is one flat syllable with no English "tahn" drawl. di-FI-sil, stressed in the middle, where the accent mark says.

variations.display: Este libro no es tan caro como el otro.
variations.cue: This book isn't as expensive as the other one.
variations.changed: the adjective changed inside the frame

variations.display: No es tan fácil como parece.
variations.cue: It's not as easy as it looks.
variations.changed: the comparison made against how it seems

mistake.display: Este libro no es tan difícil que el otro.
mistake.why: Only como closes tan: tan difícil como el otro. que is what English's "than" pulls in, and it belongs to L2-M9's más and menos instead.

sentences.usage: The polite way to disagree about anything with a price or a difficulty on it — you rank rather than reject.
sentences.mnemonic: tan opens it, como closes it.

sentences.display: Estoy de acuerdo contigo. No estoy de acuerdo con tu jefe.
sentences.cue: I agree with you. I don't agree with your boss.
sentences.literal: I-am of accord with-you. Not I-am of accord with your boss.

words.note: Agreement is a position you are standing in, not something you do: estoy de acuerdo. There is no verb "to agree" to reach for, and de acuerdo alone answers a question.

sentences.trap: English has a verb here and Spanish has a place. Nothing in estoy de acuerdo is optional — dropping the de, or swapping estoy for soy, breaks it.
sentences.sound: es-TOY de a-KUER-do, said as one run with no stop before de. The final o is short.

variations.cue: I don't agree.
variations.changed: the negative standing on its own

variations.display: Estoy de acuerdo con mi hermana.
variations.cue: I agree with my sister.
variations.changed: who is agreed with

mistake.why: It is a position, so it takes estar: estoy de acuerdo contigo. soy would make agreeing part of who you are rather than where you stand today.

sentences.usage: Said in full when it matters and clipped to de acuerdo when it does not — the short form is the everyday one.
sentences.mnemonic: You STAND in agreement, so estar.

sentences.display: Estoy de acuerdo, aunque el libro es un poco caro.
sentences.cue: I agree, although the book is a bit expensive.
sentences.literal: I-am of accord, although the book is a little expensive.

words.note: Joins a concession to a claim, at either end of the sentence: aunque es caro, estoy de acuerdo. Here it takes the indicative, because what it concedes is a fact.

sentences.trap: aunque is one word doing what English does with two, and the sentence needs no comma the way English wants one. Both orders are ordinary.
sentences.sound: AUN-ke, with au said as one glide and the que a clean ke — no w sound anywhere in it.

variations.display: No estoy de acuerdo, aunque es interesante.
variations.cue: I don't agree, although it's interesting.
variations.changed: the concession attached to a disagreement

variations.display: Aunque es caro, creo que es bueno.
variations.cue: Although it's expensive, I think it's good.
variations.changed: the concession moved to the front

mistake.display: Estoy de acuerdo, aunque sea un poco caro.
mistake.why: At this level aunque takes the indicative for something that is true: aunque es un poco caro. The subjunctive there says "even if", about something not yet settled, and it is a later level's.

sentences.usage: The whole shape of a reasoned opinion: the position first, the reservation attached, nothing withdrawn.
sentences.mnemonic: aunque concedes a fact, so the fact stays indicative.

sentences.display: Depende de mi horario. No creo que pueda ir el sábado.
sentences.cue: It depends on my hours. I don't think I can go on Saturday.
sentences.literal: Depends of my timetable. Not I-believe that can to-go the Saturday.

words.note: A whole answer on its own, as English's "it depends" is. What it depends on always takes de: depende de mi horario, never depende en.

sentences.trap: English says "depends on" and the on is what an English speaker translates. Spanish reaches for de, and en there is audibly wrong rather than merely odd.
sentences.sound: de-PEN-de, stressed in the middle, and the two de sounds around it are identical.

variations.cue: It's up to you.
variations.changed: what it depends on made a person

variations.cue: It depends on my boss.
variations.changed: who decides it

mistake.why: depende takes de and only de: depende de mi horario. English's "depends on" is what puts en there, and it is the commonest error in the frame.

sentences.usage: The half-answer everybody gives before committing to a weekend. It softens by deferring rather than by hedging.

sentences.display: La verdad es que no sé si es tan fácil.
sentences.cue: The truth is I don't know if it's that easy.
sentences.literal: The truth is that not I-know if is so easy.

words.note: la verdad es que opens a claim you are willing to own. It softens by framing the speaker, not by weakening what comes after it.
The si inside is "whether", and it is not L1-M2's sí, "yes" — accents are letters. Taught whole here; the bare si earns its own row in the next module.

sentences.trap: si and sí are one keystroke apart and mean opposite things. No sé sí is not a typo a reader repairs; it is a different word in the sentence.
sentences.sound: la ver-DA es ke, with the final d of verdad barely said at all — closer to a soft th than to an English d.

variations.cue: I don't know if I can go.
variations.changed: the frame over a plan instead of an opinion

variations.display: La verdad es que estoy cansado.
variations.cue: The truth is I'm tired.
variations.changed: the truth frame over a feeling

mistake.display: No sé sí es tan fácil.
mistake.why: The whether-si carries no accent: no sé si es tan fácil. sí with one is L1-M2's yes, and writing it turns the doubt into an agreement.

sentences.usage: How a Spanish speaker disagrees with a room. la verdad es que announces that the next thing is honest rather than that it is harsh.

sentences.display: Me parece interesante, aunque no creo que sea fácil.
sentences.cue: It seems interesting to me, although I don't think it's easy.
sentences.literal: To-me seems interesting, although not I-believe that be easy.

words.note: One ending for both genders: un libro interesante, una película interesante. It reads exactly as English reads it, and the plural is interesantes.

sentences.trap: me parece takes an adjective with nothing between them. The que only arrives when a whole clause follows, and this item has one of each.
sentences.sound: in-te-re-SAN-te, five syllables and the stress late — nothing like the English word's front-loaded shape.

variations.cue: It seems interesting to me.
variations.changed: the concession dropped

variations.display: Creo que es interesante, aunque es difícil.
variations.cue: I think it's interesting, although it's hard.
variations.changed: creo que back in the indicative on both halves

mistake.why: me parece takes the adjective directly — me parece interesante — and me parece que needs a whole clause after it: me parece que es interesante.

sentences.usage: The module in one line: a soft frame, a concession, and a doubt that reaches the verb. Nothing here is new except the adjective.
sentences.mnemonic: An adjective needs no que; a clause does.
